messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Six months ago, Arthur was assisting his brother-in-law lower a heavy equipment crate into the basement of his own home. He had positioned himself to bear the load, but the strap slipped. The crate struck the man’s thigh with a force that left a permanent scar and ended the brother-in-law’s ability to return to his former work. The memory of that impact remained sharp, anchored by the sudden terror that had flooded him in the moment and the heavy guilt that followed. In the weeks since, those memories did not settle. They arrived without warning as sudden pieces—the sound of the strap giving way, the sickening thud, the clinical silence of the hospital waiting room—each fragment carrying the same terror and guilt he felt as if it were happening now. He could not dismiss them, nor could he predict when they would surface. His body adjusted to a new baseline. He sat awake long past midnight, convinced that drifting off would leave him defenseless. His muscles stayed knotted at the kitchen table and at his teller window. He was always watchful, scanning the bank floor for irregularities, for sudden movements. When he tried to rest at home, he was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His shoulders remained raised, his breathing shallow, as though the basement were still echoing around him. He had come to believe his capacity for care had been compromised, that his body no longer trusted its own commands. He simply accepted that he would always be on guard. At the bank, the environment pressed against his routines. The teller line required him to face outward, hands on the counter, ready for the next transaction. The morning rush brought a steady stream of customers pressing forward, their voices overlapping with the hum of the vault door. When a regular customer reached across the polished wood to hand over an envelope, the unprepared touch sent a sharp jolt up his arms. He would set the transaction down, step back behind the glass, and wait until his pulse settled. Stress at the branch—long queues, a ringing phone, a supervisor asking about vault discrepancies—made his vision tunnel. He told himself he was managing, but at home, he flinched when his wife placed a hand on his shoulder. She was family, yet the closeness made his chest tighten. He stopped volunteering for weekend projects or community events. He watched himself struggle to keep pace with his old life, and every misstep confirmed his quiet conviction: he was inadequate. He did not think he would ever be the man he used to be. His reactions to the everyday world felt like proof that he was a lousy coper, that the damage was permanent. He had stopped trying to explain his exhaustion to his coworkers; he simply showed up, balanced his till with careful hands, and retreated. It was his wife who finally asked him to make an appointment, noting how he jumped at the closing of the bank’s front door and how he barely ate with her anymore. Arthur went because he wanted the terror to stop, because he needed to know if he could ever feel safe in his own skin again. He was most afraid that the man who caused the injury would always be the only man he knew how to be, but he hoped, quietly, that someone might help him learn how to carry the weight without breaking.
